questions.stem:
The cost function of a firm which produces plastic plates is shown in the table below. Use the information in the table to answer the questions that follow:
Output (in cartons) / Total Variable Cost (TVC) / Total Cost (TC) / Average Cost (AC) / Marginal Cost (MC):
0 / - / 100 / - / -
1 / 250 / 350 / 350 / -
2 / 450 / P / 275 / 200
3 / 575 / 675 / R / 125
4 / 600 / 700 / 175 / 25
5 / 675 / Q / 155 / 75
6 / 825 / 925 / S / 150
(a) (i) What is average fixed cost (AFC)? [2 marks]
(ii) Calculate the average fixed cost at output levels 1 to 6. [6 marks]
(b) Calculate the values P, Q, R and S. [8 marks]
(c) Why does the average fixed cost decline as output increases? [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) AFC is total fixed cost divided by the quantity of output (TFC/Q), i.e. fixed cost per unit of output
6 marks: (a)(ii) TFC = 100 (TC at zero output); AFC: 1 = 100, 2 = 50, 3 = 33.33, 4 = 25, 5 = 20, 6 = 16.67 (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b) P = TVC + TFC = 450 + 100 = 550
2 marks: (b) Q = 675 + 100 = 775
2 marks: (b) R = TC/Q = 675/3 = 225
2 marks: (b) S = 925/6 = 154.17
4 marks: (c) total fixed cost is constant whatever the output, so as output increases the same fixed cost is spread over more units and the fixed cost per unit falls continuously
questions.explanation: (a)(i) Average fixed cost is total fixed cost divided by output (AFC = TFC/Q). (ii) Total fixed cost is 100, the total cost at zero output. AFC = 100/1 = 100; 100/2 = 50; 100/3 = 33.33; 100/4 = 25; 100/5 = 20; 100/6 = 16.67. (b) P = 450 + 100 = 550 (check: 550/2 = 275). Q = 675 + 100 = 775 (check: 775/5 = 155). R = 675/3 = 225. S = 925/6 = 154.17. (c) Fixed cost does not change with output, so as more units are produced the same fixed cost is spread over a larger output and the cost per unit keeps falling.

questions.stem:
The diagram below represents the situation in a regulated market. [Diagram described in words: a downward-sloping demand curve DD and an upward-sloping supply curve SS intersect at price P0 and quantity Q0. A price Pc is marked above P0; at Pc the demand curve gives quantity Q1 and the supply curve gives quantity Q2 (Q1 < Q0 < Q2). A price Pk is marked below P0; at Pk the supply curve gives quantity Q1 and the demand curve gives quantity Q2.]
Use the diagram to answer the questions that follow:
(a) What do P0 and Q0 represent? [2 marks]
(b) What would you call the regulated price Pc? Explain your answer. [3 marks]
(c) What is Q1Q2? [2 marks]
(d) What is Pk? [2 marks]
(e) In what circumstances would a commodity be sold at Pk? [3 marks]
(f) Name two commodities whose market situation can be represented by the diagram. [2 marks]
(g) State three measures that can be taken to make the regulated price effective. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) P0 is the equilibrium price and Q0 the equilibrium quantity, where demand equals supply
3 marks: (b) Pc is a minimum (floor) price, because it is fixed by government above the equilibrium price so that price cannot legally fall below it
2 marks: (c) Q1Q2 is the excess supply (surplus) at Pc, since quantity supplied (Q2) exceeds quantity demanded (Q1); at Pk it is excess demand (shortage)
2 marks: (d) Pk is a maximum (ceiling) price fixed below the equilibrium price
3 marks: (e) when government fixes a maximum price, e.g. during scarcity, war or inflation, to protect consumers/low-income earners from high prices of essential goods
2 marks: (f) any two, 1 mark each: agricultural produce (e.g. cocoa, rice, maize under guaranteed minimum prices); petroleum products; essential drugs; rent/housing; minimum wage for labour; fertilizer
6 marks: (g) any three, 2 marks each: rationing/issue of coupons to share limited supply; government purchasing and storing surpluses (buffer stock) at the minimum price; heavy penalties/enforcement against violators; price control boards and inspectors; subsidies to producers; government's direct distribution of the commodity
questions.explanation: (a) P0 and Q0 are the equilibrium price and quantity, where demand equals supply. (b) Pc is a minimum (floor) price. It is fixed above the equilibrium price to protect producers, and the price may not fall below it. (c) At Pc producers supply Q2 but consumers buy only Q1, so Q1Q2 is the excess supply (surplus). (d) Pk is a maximum (ceiling) price, set below equilibrium. (e) Goods are sold at Pk when government imposes a maximum price to protect consumers, especially in times of scarcity, war or inflation and for essential goods. At Pk quantity demanded (Q2) exceeds quantity supplied (Q1), a shortage. (f) Agricultural produce such as cocoa or rice (minimum prices), and petroleum products, rent or essential drugs (maximum prices). (g) The regulated price can be made effective by rationing the limited supply, government buying and storing surpluses at the minimum price, and strict enforcement with penalties for offenders, supported by subsidies or direct government distribution.

questions.stem:
(a) Distinguish between underemployment and disguised unemployment. [4 marks]
(b) Outline any four measures that can be adopted by the government of your country to solve the problem of unemployment. [16 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a) underemployment: a worker is employed below his full capacity/qualification or for fewer hours than he is willing to work
2 marks: (a) disguised unemployment: more workers are engaged on a job than necessary, so the marginal productivity of the extra workers is zero; removing them would not reduce output (common in family farming)
16 marks: (b) four measures, 4 marks each: expansion of industries/industrialisation to create jobs; development of agriculture and rural areas to reduce rural-urban migration; encouraging self-employment through skills acquisition and soft loans to small businesses; vocational and technical education matching skills to needs; expansionary fiscal and monetary policies (public works, lower interest rates); attracting foreign investment; population control
questions.explanation: (a) Underemployment exists when people work below their full capacity, for example a graduate doing an unskilled job or someone working fewer hours than he wants. Disguised unemployment exists when more people are employed on a task than necessary, so the extra workers add nothing to output (their marginal product is zero), as in family farms. (b) Government can expand industries and public works to create jobs. It can develop agriculture and rural infrastructure to keep people productively employed in rural areas. It can promote self-employment through skills acquisition programmes and soft loans to small businesses. It can reform education towards vocational and technical skills. It can also use expansionary fiscal and monetary policy and attract foreign investment.

questions.stem:
(a) What are producer goods? [4 marks]
(b) Explain any four advantages of using capital in production. [16 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) goods that are not consumed directly but are used to produce other goods and services, e.g. machines, tools, factory buildings, raw materials (capital goods)
16 marks: (b) four advantages, 4 marks each: increases output/productivity of labour; makes mass production and economies of scale possible; improves quality and standardisation of goods; reduces cost per unit of production; saves time and reduces drudgery; enables specialisation and division of labour; makes possible tasks that cannot be done by hand
questions.explanation: (a) Producer goods (capital goods) are goods used to produce other goods and services rather than to satisfy wants directly, such as machines, tools, factory buildings and raw materials. (b) Capital increases the productivity of labour, so output rises. It makes mass production possible, so the firm enjoys economies of scale and lower unit costs. It improves the quality and uniformity of products. It saves time and reduces hard manual labour. It also makes possible work that could not be done by hand, such as drilling for oil.

questions.stem:
(a) Define supply. [3 marks]
(b) With the aid of a diagram, explain what is meant by a change in supply. [8 marks]
(c) Explain any three factors that cause changes in supply. [9 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) supply is the quantity of a commodity that producers are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price and time
4 marks: (b) a change in supply is a shift of the whole supply curve caused by factors other than the commodity's own price: more is supplied at every price (increase, shift to the right) or less (decrease, shift to the left)
4 marks: (b) correct diagram: price on vertical axis, quantity on horizontal; original supply curve S0 with shifted curves S1 (right) and/or S2 (left), showing quantity changing at the same price
9 marks: (c) three factors, 3 marks each: cost of production/prices of factors; technology; prices of related goods; weather/natural factors (for agricultural produce); government policy (taxes and subsidies); number of producers; expectations of future prices; objectives of the firm
questions.explanation: (a) Supply is the quantity of a commodity that producers are willing and able to offer for sale at a particular price and time. (b) A change in supply is a shift of the whole supply curve caused by factors other than the price of the good. An increase in supply shifts the curve to the right, from S0 to S1, so more is offered at every price. A decrease shifts it to the left, so less is offered at every price. The diagram has price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, with S0 and the shifted curves; at a given price P the quantity moves from Q0 to Q1. (c) Supply changes with the cost of production (higher input prices reduce supply); with technology (better methods increase supply); with government policy (taxes reduce supply, subsidies increase it); with weather, especially for farm produce; and with the prices of related goods and producers' expectations.

questions.stem:
(a) What is a customs union? [4 marks]
(b) Explain any four ways in which a customs union can speed up the economic growth of its members. [16 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) a form of economic integration in which member countries remove tariffs and other trade barriers among themselves and adopt a common external tariff against non-members
16 marks: (b) four ways, 4 marks each: wider market enabling large-scale production and economies of scale; increased trade among members (trade creation); specialisation according to comparative advantage; increased competition leading to efficiency; attraction of foreign investment; improved bargaining power with the rest of the world; joint development of infrastructure; transfer of technology and free movement of factors
questions.explanation: (a) A customs union is an arrangement in which member countries remove tariffs and other barriers on trade among themselves and impose a common external tariff on goods from non-members. (b) It enlarges the market, so firms can produce on a large scale and enjoy economies of scale. It creates trade among members and encourages specialisation according to comparative advantage. It increases competition, which improves efficiency. It attracts foreign investment into the bigger market. It also strengthens members' bargaining power in world trade and encourages joint infrastructure projects and the transfer of technology.

questions.stem:
(a) What is standard of living? [4 marks]
(b) Highlight four problems in using national income data in comparing the standard of living between two countries. [16 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) the level of material welfare/well-being of the people of a country, measured by the quantity and quality of goods and services they consume (often indicated by per capita income)
16 marks: (b) four problems, 4 marks each: differences in currencies and exchange rates; differences in income distribution; differences in population size and structure; differences in methods of computing national income and inaccurate data; differences in the composition of output (e.g. defence vs consumer goods); non-market/subsistence production not recorded; differences in tastes, climate and needs; differences in price levels
questions.explanation: (a) The standard of living is the level of material well-being of the people, shown by the quantity and quality of goods and services they enjoy; it is often measured by income per head. (b) National income data are hard to compare between countries because the countries use different currencies and exchange rates may not reflect purchasing power. Income may be distributed very unequally. Methods of calculation and the accuracy of data differ, and subsistence output is often unrecorded. The composition of output differs, e.g. heavy defence spending. Population size, tastes, climate and needs also differ.

questions.stem:
(a) What is a legal tender? [4 marks]
(b) Describe any four attributes that an item must possess to act as a medium of exchange. [16 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) money which, by law, must be accepted in settlement of debts and payment for goods and services, e.g. coins and bank notes issued by the central bank
16 marks: (b) four attributes, 4 marks each: general acceptability; portability (easy to carry); divisibility into smaller units; durability; homogeneity/uniformity; relative scarcity (limited supply); stability of value; difficulty to counterfeit (recognisability)
questions.explanation: (a) Legal tender is money that the law requires people to accept in payment of debts, such as the coins and notes issued by the central bank. (b) To serve as a medium of exchange an item must be generally acceptable to everyone. It must be portable, easy to carry about. It must be divisible into smaller units for small payments. It must be durable and not perish. It should also be homogeneous, relatively scarce, stable in value and hard to forge.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain any three contributions of the agricultural sector to the economy of your country. [12 marks]
(b) Outline any two constraints on agricultural production in your country. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
12 marks: (a) three contributions, 4 marks each: provides food for the population; provides raw materials for industries; provides employment for a large part of the labour force; earns foreign exchange through exports; source of government revenue; provides market for industrial goods; contributes to national income (GDP)
8 marks: (b) two constraints, 4 marks each: use of crude tools/low mechanisation; inadequate credit facilities; poor transport and storage facilities; land tenure system; pests, diseases and bad weather; low prices/poor marketing; rural-urban migration of young labour; inadequate extension services
questions.explanation: (a) Agriculture provides food for the growing population. It supplies raw materials such as cotton, cocoa and palm oil to local industries. It employs a large part of the labour force, especially in rural areas. It also earns foreign exchange through exports and provides government revenue, as well as a market for industrial goods. (b) Production is limited by the use of crude tools and little mechanisation, inadequate credit for farmers, poor roads and storage facilities, the land tenure system, and pests, diseases and unreliable rainfall.

questions.stem:
(a) What is the difference between the following terms?
(i) ad valorem tax and specific tax; [4 marks]
(ii) a progressive tax and a regressive tax. [4 marks]
(b) Give any three reasons why the government of your country imposes indirect taxes. [12 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) ad valorem tax is levied as a percentage of the value (price) of a commodity
2 marks: (a)(i) specific tax is a fixed amount per unit (quantity, weight, volume) of a commodity regardless of its value
2 marks: (a)(ii) progressive tax: the rate (proportion of income paid) rises as income rises
2 marks: (a)(ii) regressive tax: the rate falls as income rises, so the poor pay a larger proportion of their income than the rich
12 marks: (b) three reasons, 4 marks each: to raise revenue for government; to discourage consumption of harmful goods (e.g. tobacco, alcohol); to protect infant/home industries from imports; to correct balance of payments deficits; to redistribute income (taxing luxuries); to control inflation; difficult to evade and easy to collect
questions.explanation: (a)(i) An ad valorem tax is a percentage of the value of a good (e.g. 5% VAT), while a specific tax is a fixed amount per unit of quantity regardless of value (e.g. N10 per litre). (ii) Under a progressive tax the rate rises as income rises, so the rich pay a higher proportion of their income. Under a regressive tax the rate falls as income rises, so the poor pay a higher proportion. (b) Government imposes indirect taxes to raise revenue, since they are easy to collect and hard to evade. They discourage consumption of harmful goods such as alcohol and tobacco. Import duties protect local industries and help correct a balance of payments deficit. Indirect taxes can also reduce income inequality by taxing luxuries, and can help control inflation by reducing spending.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain any four objectives of public finance. [12 marks]
(b) Give two reasons for the increase in government expenditure in your country in recent years. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
12 marks: (a) four objectives, 3 marks each: to raise revenue to finance government activities; to provide public/social goods and services (defence, education, health); to redistribute income and wealth; to promote economic growth and development; to achieve price stability/control inflation; to promote full employment; to correct balance of payments disequilibrium; to regulate the economy/protect local industries
8 marks: (b) two reasons, 4 marks each: rapid population growth; expansion of social services (education, health); increased defence and security spending; inflation (rising cost of goods and services); servicing of public debt; infrastructure development; increased cost of governance/salaries; creation of new states and local governments
questions.explanation: (a) Public finance aims to raise revenue for government activities; to provide public goods and social services such as defence, education and health; to redistribute income and wealth more equitably; to promote economic growth and full employment; and to stabilise prices and the balance of payments. (b) Government expenditure has risen because of rapid population growth, which requires more schools, hospitals and infrastructure. Inflation has raised the cost of goods and services. Other causes are higher security spending, debt servicing, and the higher cost of running government, including salaries.

questions.stem:
(a) Outline any three achievements of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC). [12 marks]
(b) State any two problems facing the organization. [8 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
12 marks: (a) three achievements, 4 marks each: increased oil revenues of member states (e.g. through the price increases of the 1970s); stabilisation of world oil prices through production quotas; increased control of members over their oil resources (participation/nationalisation of oil companies); bargaining power against multinational oil companies and consumer countries; OPEC Fund for International Development giving aid/loans to developing countries; training and exchange of technical information
8 marks: (b) two problems, 4 marks each: quota violations/over-production by members; competition from non-OPEC producers; development of alternative energy sources and conservation by consumers; political disagreements and wars among members; fluctuations in world oil prices and demand; dependence on Western technology
questions.explanation: (a) OPEC has raised the oil revenues of its members, notably through the price increases of the 1970s. Its production quotas have helped to stabilise world oil prices. It has helped members gain greater control over their oil resources from the multinational oil companies, and strengthened their bargaining power. Through the OPEC Fund for International Development it gives loans and aid to developing countries. (b) Members often exceed their quotas, which weakens prices. OPEC also faces competition from non-OPEC producers, the development of alternative energy sources, and political conflicts among its members.
